sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Don't tell me of your sorrow and repentance girl—you've broke my heart—married hey? and privately too—and to a lord into the bargain! So, when you can hide it no longer, you condescend to tell me—think you that the wealth and title of Lord Austencourt, can silence the fears of a fond father's heart? Why should a lord marry a poor girl like you in private, if his intentions were honorable?—Who should restrain him from publicly avowing his wife?

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: My dearest father—have but a little patience, and I'll explain all—

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Who was present besides the parson at your wedding?—

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: There was our neighbour, the attorney Sir—and one of his clerks—and they were all—

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: My heart sinks within me—but mark me. You may remember I was not always what now I seem to be.—I yesterday received intelligence, which but for this discovery had shed a gleam of joy over my remaining days—as it is, should your husband prove the villain I suspect him, that intelligence will afford me an opportunity to resume a character in life, which shall make this monster Lord tremble!—the wrongs of Abel Growse, the poor but upright man, might have been pleaded in vain to him, but as I shall soon appear, it shall go hard but I will make the great man shrink before me, even in his plenitude of pride and power.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: You terrify me Sir—indeed you do!

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: And so I would—I would prepare you for the worst that may befal us—for should this man, this Lord, who calls himself your husband—

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Dearest father what can you mean—who calls himself my husband—he is my husband.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: If he is your husband, how does he dare to pay his addresses, as he now publicly does, to the daughter of Sir Willoughby Worrett, our neighbour. I may be mistaken—I'm in the midst here of old acquaintances, tho' in this guise they know me not—they shall soon see me amongst them—not a word of this I charge you; to your faithful friend Mrs. Richland, alone confide my doubts, and act as she directs—come girl—this lord shall own you. If he does not, we will seek our remedy in those laws which are at once the best guardians of our rights and the surest avengers of our wrongs—

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: A Parlour in Sir W. Worrett's House.
The Breakfast prepared—Urn, &c. Sir Willoughby reading the Newspaper. He rises and rings the Bell—then pulls out his Watch.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Three quarters of an hour since breakfast was first announced to my wife!—my patience is exhausted. Oh wedlock, wedlock! why did I ever venture again into thy holy state—of misery! —of all the taxes laid on mankind by respect to society and the influence of example, no one is so burthensome as that which obliges a man to submit to a thousand ills at home, rather than be suspected of being a bad husband abroad!—
Go to your lady—

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: I told her ladyship five times before, Sir Willoughby, that breakfast was waiting.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Then tell her once more, and that will make six, and say I earnestly request the favor she will hasten to breakfast, as while she stays, I starve.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Willoughby—but she'll stop the longer for the message.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: My wife is the very devil—it seems that she'd be miserable if she didn't think me happy— yet her tenderness is my eternal torment—her affection puts me in a fidget, and her fondness in a fever.

sp.speaker: Serv.
sp.p: My lady says she wont detain you a moment, Sir Willoughby.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: The old answer!—Then she's so nervous! A nervous wife is worse than a perpetual blister; and then, as the man says in the play, your nervous patients are always ailing but never die! Zounds! why do I bear it? 'tis my folly, my weakness, to dread the censure of the world, and to sacrifice every comfort of my fire side, to the ideal advantage of being esteemed a good husband.

Hark?—now she begins her morning work, giving more orders in a minute than can be executed in a month—and teizing my daughter to death to teach her to keep her temper!—yet every body congratulates me on having so good a wife!—every body envies me so excellent an economist!—every body thinks me the happiest man alive! and nobody knows what a miserable mortal I am!
—and harkye William—
tell the coachman to bring the chariot in a quarter of an hour—and William— run with these books immediately to the Rector's —and William—bring up breakfast this moment.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Yes, my lady—
—Lord have mercy upon us!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: My dear Sir Willoughby—I beg a thousand pardons, but you are always so indulgent that you really spoil me—I'm sure you must think me a tiresome creature.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No—no, my life—not at all.—I should be very ungrateful if I didn't value you just exactly as highly as you deserve.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: I certainly deserve a good scolding—I do, indeed.—I think if you scolded me a little I should behave better.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Well, then, as you encourage me, my-love —I must own that a little more punctuality would greatly heighten the zest of your society.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: And yet, Sir Willoughby, you must acknowledge that my time is ever dedicated to that proper vigilance which the superintendance of so large an establishment undoubtedly requires.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why, true, my-love;—but somehow, I can't help thinking, that as my fortune is so ample, it is quite unnecessary that you should undergo so much fatigue: for instance, I do think that the wife of a baronet of 12,000l. a year owes it to her rank to be otherwise employed than in hunting after the house maid, or sacrificing her time in the store-room in counting candles, or weighing out soap, starch, powder-blue, and brown sugar!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: This is unkind, Sir Willoughby —this is very unkind—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: So! as usual, here's a breeze springing up!—What the devil shall I say to soothe her?— Wife! wife! you drive me mad! You first beg me to scold you, and then are offended because I obligingly comply with your request.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: No, Sir Willoughby—I am only surprized that you should so little know the value of a wife, who daily degrades herself for your advantage.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's the very thing I complain of. You do degrade yourself—your economy, my-life, is downright parsimony; your vigilance is suspicion; your management is meanness; and you fidget your servants till you make them fretful, and then prudently discharge them because they will live with you no longer. Hey! odslife, I must soothe her! for if company comes and finds her in this humour, my dear-bought reputation as a good husband is lost for ever.—
Come, come—my dear Lady Worrett, let us go to breakfast—Come
let us talk of something else—Come, take your tea.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Send William to speak to me.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Where's Helen?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: I have desired her to copy a few articles into the family receipt book, before breakfast; for as her marriage will so shortly take place, it is necessary she should complete her studies.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: What—she's at work, I suppose, on the third folio volume.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: The fifth I believe.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Heaven defend us!—I don't blame it— I don't censure it at all—but I believe the case is rather unprecedented for an heiress of 12,000l. a year to leave to posterity in her own hand writing, five folio volumes of recipes, for pickling, preserving, potting, and pastry, for stewing and larding, making ketchup and sour krout, oyster patties, barbecued pies, jellies, jams, soups, sour-sauce and sweetmeats.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Oh Sir Willoughby, if young ladies of the present day paid more attention to such substantial acquirements, we should have better wives and better husbands.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why that is singularly just—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Yes, if women were taught to find amusement in domestic duties instead of seeking it at a circulating library, assemblies and balls, we should hear of fewer appeals to Doctor's Commons and the Court of King's Bench.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why that is undeniably true
and now as we have a moment uninterrupted by family affairs—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Is the carriage come?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: No, my lady.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Have you carried the books?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: No, my lady.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Then go and hasten the coachman.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: No my lady—yes my lady.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: And William—send up Tiffany to Miss Helen's room, and bid her say we expect her at breakfast.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Miss Helen has been in the Park these two hours.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: How! in the Park these two hours? Impossible—send Tiffany to seek her.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Yes, my lady.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: So, as usual, risen with the lark, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Her disobedience will break my heart!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Zounds, I shall go mad! here's a mother-in-law going to break my heart, because my daughter prefers a walk in the morning to writing culinary secrets into a fat folio family receipt-book!!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Sir Willoughby, Sir Willoughby, it is you who encourage her in disregarding my orders.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No such thing, Lady Worrett, no such thing! but if the girl likes to bring home a pair of ruddy cheeks from a morning walk, I don't see why she is to be balked of her fancy.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Ruddy cheeks indeed! such robust health is becoming only in dairy-maids.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, I know your taste to a T; a consumption is always a key to your tender heart— and an interesting pallid countenance will at any time unlock the door to your best affections—but I must be excused if I prefer seeing my daughter with the rosy glow of health upon her cheek, rather than the sickly imitations of art, which bloom on the surface alone, while the fruit withers and decays beneath—but zounds, dont speak so loud—here's somebody coming, and they'll think we are quarelling.
So here comes our madcap.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Good morning—good morning. Here papa, look what a beautiful posy of wild flowers I have gathered—See! the dew is still upon them— how lovely they are!—to my fancy now, these uncultivated productions of nature have more charms than the whole garden can equal—why can we not all be like these flowers, simple and inartificial, with the stamp of nature and truth upon us?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Romantic stuff,—but how comes it, Miss Helen, that my orders are thus disobeyed?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why lord, mamma, I'll tell you how it was—but first I must eat my breakfast—so I'll sit down and tell you all about it.

In the first place I rose at six—and remembering I was to copy out the whole catalogue of sweetmeats, and as I hate all sweet things—some sugar, if you please, papa—I determined to take one run round the park before I sat down to my morning's work—so taking a crust of bread and a glass of cold water, which I love better than—some tea if you please mamma—any thing in the world!— out I flew like a lapwing—stop'd at the Dairy, and—some cream if you please, papa—down to the meadows and gathered my nosegay, and then bounded home, with a heart full of gaiety, and a rare appetite—for—some roll and butter, if you please, mamma.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Daughter, this levity of character is unbecoming your sex, and even your age—you see none of this offensive flightiness in me—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Come, come, my dear Lady Worrett, Helen's gaiety is natural—Helen, my love—I have charming news for you—every thing is at last arranged between Lord Austencourt and me respecting your marriage.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why now, if mamma-in-law had said this, I should have thought she meant to make me as grave as herself.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: In expectation that Helen will behave as becomes her in this most important affair of her life, I consent to pass over her negligence this morning in regard to my favorite receipts.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I hate all receipts—sweet, bitter, and, sour.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Then we will now talk of a husband.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I hate all husbands—sweet, bitter, and sour.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Whoo! Helen my love, you should not contradict your mamma.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: My dear papa—I don't contradict her; but I will not marry Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: This is too much for my weak nerves— I leave you, Sir Willoughby to arrange this affair, while I hasten to attend to my domestic duties.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's right—you'd better leave her to me—I'll manage her, I warrant— let me assist you—there—I'll soon settle this business.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Now, my dear papa, are you really of the same opinion as her ladyship?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Exactly.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Ha! Ha! Lud! but that's comical— What—both think alike?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Precisely!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: That's very odd! I believe it's the first time you've agreed in opinion since you were made one! But I'm quite sure you never can wish me to marry a man I do not love.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why no—certainly not—but you will love him—indeed you must. It's my wife's wish you know, and so I wish it of course—Come, come, in this one trifling matter you must oblige us.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Well, as you think it only a trifling matter, and as I think it of importance enough to make me miserable, I'm sure you'll give up the point.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why no—you are mistaken—to be sure I might have given it up—but my Lady Worrett you know—but that's no matter—marriage is a 51duty, and 'tis incumbent on parents to see their children settled in that—happy—state.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Have you found that state so happy, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why—yes—that is—Hey? happy! certainly —doesn't every body say so? And what every body says must be true. However, that's not to the purpose—a connection with the family of Lord Austencourt is particularly desirable.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Not to me, I assure you, papa!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Our estates join so charmingly to one another.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: But sure, that's no reason we should be joined to one another!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: But their contiguity seems to invite a union by a marriage between you.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Then pray, papa, let the stewards marry the estates, and give me a separate maintenance.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Helen, Helen! I see you are bent on disobedience to my Lady Worrett's wishes— Zounds! you don't see me disobedient to her wishes—but I know whereabouts your objection lies;—that giddy, dissipated, young fellow, his cousin Charles, the son of Sir Rowland Austencourt, has filled your head with nonsensical notions and chimeras of happiness—thank heaven, however, he's far enough off at sea.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And I think, Sir, that because a man is fighting our battles abroad, he ought not to be the less dear to those whom his courage enables to live in tranquility at home.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's very true—
but I have an unanswerable objection to all you can say. Lord Austencourt is rich, and Charles is a beggar! besides, Sir Rowland himself prefers Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: More shame for him—his partial feelings to his nephew, and unnatural disregard of his son, have long since made me hate him—in short—you are for money, and chuse Lord Austencourt—I am for love, and prefer his poor cousin.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Then, once for all—(as my Lady Worrett must be obeyed)—I no longer consult you on the subject, and it only remains for you to retain the affection of an indulgent father by complying with my will—(I mean my wife's) or to abandon my protection.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I won't marry him, papa, I won't—nor I won't cry, tho' I've a great mind—A plague of all money, say I. Oh! what a grievous misfortune it is to be born with 12,000l. a year! but if I can't marry the man I like, I won't marry at all, that's determined; and every body knows the firmness of a woman's resolution,—when she resolves on contradiction.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Boxes round the shelves—O'Dedimus discovered writing at an office table—a few papers and parchments, &c.

sp.speaker: O'Dedimus.
sp.p: There! I think I've expressed my meaning quite plainly—

“Farmer Flail —I'm instructed by Lord Austencourt, your landlord, to inform you, by word of letter, that if you can't afford to pay the additional rent for your farm, you must turn out.” (I think that's clear enough) “As to your putting in the plea of a large family, we cannot allow that as a set off; because, when a man can't afford to support seven children with decency, he ought not to trouble himself to get them.”—I think that's plain English—“Your humble servant, Cornelius O'Dedimus, Attorney at Law.”“P. S. You may show this letter to his lordship, to convince him I have done my duty; but as I don't mean one word of it, if you'll come to me privately I'll see what can be done for you without his knowing any thing of the matter,”— and I think that's plain English.

div.stage: Enter Gamekeeper with a Countryman in custody.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Well, friend, and what are you?

sp.speaker: Countryman.
sp.p: I be's a poacher! So my lord's gamekeeper here do say.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: A poacher! Faith that's honest!

sp.speaker: Gamekeeper.
sp.p: I caught him before day-light on the manor. I took away his gun, and shot his dog.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That was bravely done! So you must pamper your long stomach with pheasants and partridges, and be damn'd to ye! Will you prefer paying five pounds now, or three months hard labour in the house of correction?

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: Thank ye, Sir,—I don't prefer either, Sir.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: You must go before the justice—he'll exhort you, and commit ye!

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: Eees, I do know that extortion and commission, and such like, be the office of the justice; but I'll have a bit of law, please punch!—He ha' kill'd my poor dog that I lov'd like one o'my own children, and I've gotten six of 'em, Lord bless 'em.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Six dogs!

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: Dogs! No! children, mun.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Six children! Och, the fruitful sinner!

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: My wife be a pain's-taking woman, Sir!—We ha' had this poor dear dog from a puppy.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Shut your ugly mouth, you babbler— Six children!—Oh! we must make an example of this fellow—an't I the village lawyer? and an't I the terror of all the rogues in the parish?
You must plead “not guilty.”

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: But I tell you, if that be guilt, I be guilty.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Why, you blundering booby, if you plead guilty, how will I ever be able to prove you innocent.

sp.speaker: Countrym.
sp.p: Guilty or innocent, I'll have the law of him, by gum!—he has shot my poor old mongrel, and taken away my musket; and I've lost my day's drilling, and I'll make him pay for it.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: A mongrel, and a musket! by St. Patrick, Mr. Gamekeeper, and you have nately set your foot in it!

sp.speaker: Gamekeeper.
sp.p: Why, Sir, its a bad affair, Sir— 'twas so dark, I couldn't see; and when I discovered my mistake, I offered him a shilling to make it up, and he refused it!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Harkye, Mr. Gamekeeper; he has one action against ye for his dog, and another for false imprisonment
. I love to see the laws enforced with justice.—
but I'll always help a poor man to stand up against oppression—
He has got you on the hip, and so go out and settle it between yourselves, and do you take care of yourself:
and do you make the best of your bargain.

div.stage: Parish Officer brings forward the Sailor.

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: Here's a vagrant—I found him begging without a pass.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Take him before his worship directly— the sturdy rogue ought to be punished.

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.p: Please your honor, I'm a sailor.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And if you're a sailor, a'nt you ashamed to own it—a begging sailor is a disgrace to an honorable profession, for which the country has provided an asylum as glorious as it is deserved!

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.p: Why so it has—but I an't bound for Greenwich yet!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Why you're disabled I see!

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.p: Disabled! what for? why I've only lost one arm yet—bless ye I'm no beggar. I was going to see my Nancy thirty miles further on the road, and meeting some old messmates, we had a cann o'grog together; one cann brought on another, and then we got drinking the King's health, and the Navy, and then this Admiral, and then t'other Admiral, 'till at last we had so many gallant heroes to drink, that we were all drunk afore we came to the reck'ning. So your honor, as my messmates had none o'the rhino, I paid all; and then you know they had a long journey upwards, and no biscuit aboard: so I lent one a little, and another a little, 'till at last I found I had no coin left in my locker for myself except a cracked teaster that Nancy gave me;—and I couldn't spend that you know, tho' I had been starving!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And so you begg'd?

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.p: Begg'd, no! I just axed for a bit of bread and a mug o'water. That's no more than one Christian ought to give another, and if you call that begging, why I beg to differ in opinion.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: According to the act, you are a vagrant, and the justice may commit ye;

—lookye, Mr. Officer—you're in the wrong box here. Can't you see plain enough, by his having lost an arm, that he earns a livelihood by the work of his hands—so lest he should be riotous for being detained, let me advise you to be off. I'll send him off after you with a flea in his ear—the other way.

sp.speaker: Officer.
sp.p: Thank ye Sir—thank ye—I'm much obliged to you for your advice, Sir, and shall take it, and so my service to you.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Take this my honest lad,
, say nothing about it, and give my service to Nancy.

sp.speaker: Sailor.
sp.p: Why now, heaven bless your honor for ever; and if ever you're in distress, and I'm within sight of signals, why hang out your blue lights; and if I don't bear down to your assistance, may my gun be primed with damp powder the first time we fire a broadside at an enemy.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Ponder!—Now will this fellow be thinking and thinking till he quite forgets what he's doing—Ponder, I say—
Here Ponder, take this letter to Farmer Flail's, and if you see Mrs. Muddle, his neighbour, give my love and duty to her.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes, yes, Sir—but at that moment, Sir, I was immers'd in thought, if I may be allow'd the expression—I was thinking of the vast difference between love and law, and yet how neatly you've spliced them together in your last instructions to your humble servant, Peter Ponder—Clerk!— Umph!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Umph! is that your manners you bear-garden? Will I never be able to larn you to behave yourself? Study me, and talk like a gentleman, and be damn'd to ye.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I study the law—I can't talk it!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Can't you? Then you'll never do—If your tongue don't run faster than your client's, how will you ever be able to bother him you booby?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I'll draw out his case—he shall read, and he'll bother himself!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: You've a notion—mind my instructions and I don't despair of seeing you at the bar one day—was that copy of a writ sarved yesterday upon Garble, the tailor?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Aye.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And sarve him right too—that's a big rogue that runs in debt wid his eyes open, and tho' he has property, refuses to pay—Is he safe?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: He was bailed by Swash, the brewer.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And was the other sarved on Shuttle, the weaver—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Aye.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Who bailed him?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Nobody, he's gone to jail.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Gone to jail! Why his poverty is owing to misfortune—he can't pay—well that's not our affair—the law must have it's course.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: So Shuttle said to his wife, as she hung crying on his shoulder.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's it, he's a sensible man—and that's more than his wife is—we've nothing to do with women's tears.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Not a bit—so they walked him off to jail in a jiffey, if I may be allowed the expression.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: To be sure, and that was right—they did their duty—tho' for sartin if a poor man can't pay his debts when he's at liberty, he won't be much nearer the mark when he's shut up in idleness in a prison.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Tho' when he that sent them there comes to make up his last account, 'tis my belief that he won't be able to shew cause why a bill shouldn't be filed against him for barbarity!— Are the writings all ready for Sir Rowland?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: All ready—shall I go now to Farmer Flail's with the letter?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Aye, and if you see Shuttle's wife in your way, give my service to her, and d'ye hear— as you're a small talker, don't let the little you say be so cursed crabbed; and if a few kind words of comfort should find their way from your heart to your tongue, don't shut your ugly mouth and keep them within your teeth: you may tell her that if she can find any body to stand up for her husband, I sha'nt be over-nice about the sufficiency of the bail—get you gone.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I shall—Let me see! Farmer Flail! —Mrs. Muddle, his neighbour!—Shuttle's wife! and a whole string of messages and memorandums —here's business enough to bother the brains of any ordinary man!—you are pleased to say, Sir, that I am too much addicted to thinking—I think not.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: By my soul if an attorney wasn't sometimes a bit of a rogue, he'd never be able to earn an honest livelihood—Oh Mr. O'Dedimus! why have you so little, when your heart could distribute so much?

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: Mr. O'Dedimus—within there!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Yes! I'm within there.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: Where are these papers?—I thought the law's delay was only felt by those who could not pay for its expedition.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: The law, Sir Rowland, is a good horse, and his pace is slow and sure, but he goes no faster because you goad him with a golden spur; but every thing is prepared, Sir—and now, Sir Rowland, I have an ugly sort of an aukward affair to mention to you—

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: Does it concern me?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: You know, Sir Rowland, at the death of my worthy friend, the late Lord Austencourt, you were left sole executor and guardian to his son, the present Lord, then an infant of three years of age.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: What does this lead to?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: With a disinterested view to benefit the estate of the minor, who came of age the other day, you some time ago embarked a capital of 14,000l. in a great undertaking.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: Proceed.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I have this morning received a letter from the agent, stating the whole concern to have failed—the partners to be bankrupts—and the property consigned to assignees not to promise, as a final dividend, more than one shilling in the pound—this letter will explain the rest.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: How! I was not prepared for this— What's to be done?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: When one loses a sum of money that isn't one's own, there's but one thing to be done.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: And what is that?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: To pay it back again!—

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: You know that to be impossible— utterly impossible.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Then, Sir Rowland, take the word of Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law, his lordship will rigidly exact the money to the uttermost farthing.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: You are fond, Sir, of throwing out these hints to his disadvantage.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I am bold to speak it—I am possessed of a secret, Sir Rowland, in regard to his lordship.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: What is it you mean?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I thought I told you it was a secret.

sp.speaker: Sir Row.
sp.p: But to me you should have no secrets that regard my family.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: With submission, Sir Rowland, his lordship is my client, as well as yourself, and I have learned from the practice of the courts, that an attorney who blabs in his business, has soon no suit to his back.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: But this affair perhaps involves my deepest interest—my character—my all is at stake.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Have done wid your pumping now—d'ye think I am a basket full of cinders, that I'm to be sifted after this fashion?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Answer but this—does it relate to Charles—my son?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sartinly, the young gentleman has a small bit of interest in the question.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: One thing more. Does it allude to a transaction which happened some years ago—am I a principal concerned in it?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Devil a ha'porth—it happened only six months past.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Enough—I breathe again.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I'm glad of that, for may-be you'll now let me breathe to tell ye that as I know Lord Austencourt's private character better than you do— my life to a bundle of parchment, he'll even arrest ye for the money.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Impossible, he cannot be such a villain!

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: What ho! is the lawyer within?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Who interrupts us?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: 'Tis the strange man that lives on the common—his name is Abel Growse—he's coming up.

sp.speaker: Sir. R.
sp.p: I'll wait till you dismiss him, for I cannot encounter any one at present—misfortunes crowd upon me—And one act of guilt has drawn the vengeance of heaven on my head, and will pursue me to the grave.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Och, if a small gale of adversity blows up such a storm as this, we shall have a pretty hurricane by-and-bye when you larn a little more of your hopeful nephew, and see his new matrimonial scheme fall to the ground like butter-milk through a sieve.

sp.speaker: Ab. Growse.
sp.p: Now, Sir—You are jackall, as I take it, to Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I am his man of business, sure enough; but didn't hear before of my promotion to the office you mention.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: You are possessed of all his secret deeds.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's a small mistake—I have but one of them, and that's the deed of settlement on Miss Helen Worrett, spinster.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Leave your quibbling, Sir, and speak plump to the point—if habit hasn't hardened your heart, and given a system to your knavery, answer me this—Lord Austencourt has privately married my daughter?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Hush!

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: You were a witness.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Has any body told you that thing?

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Will you deny it?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Will you take a friend's advice?

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: I didn't come for advice. I came to know if you will confess the fact, or whether you are villain enough to conceal it.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Have done wid your bawling—Sir Rowland's in the next room!

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Is he? then Sir Rowland shall hear me —Sir Rowland!—he shall see my daughter righted —Ho there! Sir Rowland!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Here'll be a divil of a dust kicked up presently about the ears of Mr. Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law!!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Who calls me?

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: 'Twas I!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: What is it you want, friend?

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Justice.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Justice! then you had better apply there.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: That's a mistake—he deals only in Law, 'tis to you that I appeal—your nephew, Lord Austencourt, is about to marry the daughter of Sir Willoughby Worrett.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: He is.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Never! I will save him the guilt of that crime at least!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: You are mysterious, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Perhaps I am. Briefly—your nephew is privately married to my daughter—this man was present at their union—will you see justice done me, and make him honorably proclaim his wife.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Your tale is incredible, Sir—It is sufficient however to demand attention, and I warn you lest by your folly you rouse an indignation that may crush you.

sp.speaker: Ab. Gr.
sp.p: Hear me proud man, while I warn you! my daughter is the lawful wife of lord Austencourt —double is the woe to me that she is his wife— but as it is so, he shall publicly acknowledge her—to you I look for justice and redress—see to it, Sir, or I shall speedily appear in a new character, with my wrongs in my hand, to hurl destruction on you!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: What does the fellow mean?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's just what I'm thinking—

sp.speaker: Sir. R.
sp.p: You, he said, were privy to their marriage.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Bless ye, the man's mad!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Ha! you said you had a secret respecting my nephew.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sir, if you go on so, you'll bother me!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: The fellow must be silenced—can you not contrive some means to rid us of his insolence?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sir, I shall do my duty, as my duty should be done, by Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: My nephew must not hear of this accursed loss—be secret on that head, I charge you! But in regard to this man's bold assertion, I must consult him instantly—haste and follow me to his house.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Take me wid ye, Sir; for this is such a dirty business, that I'll never be able to go through it unless you shew me the way.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Lord Austencourt—true—this is his hour for persecuting me—very well, desire Lord Austencourt to come in.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I won't marry. They all say I shall. Some girls now would sit down and sigh, and moan, as if that would mend the matter—that will never suit me? Some indeed would run away with the man they liked better—but then the only man I ever liked well enough to marry—is—I believe, run away from me. Well! that won't do! —I'll e'en laugh it off as well as I can; and tho' I won't marry his Lordship, I'll tease him as heartily as if I had been his wife for twenty years.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Helen! too lovely Helen! once more behold before you to supplicate for your love and pity, the man whom the world calls proud, but whom your beauty alone has humbled.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: They say, my Lord, that pride always has a fall some time or other.—I hope the fall of your Lordship's hasn't hurt you.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Is it possible that the amiable Helen, so famed for gentleness and goodness, can see the victim of her charms thus dejected stand before her.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Certainly not, my Lord—so pray sit down.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Will you never be for one moment serious?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Oh, yes, my Lord—I am never otherwise when I think of your Lordship's proposals—but when you are making love and fine speeches to me in person, 'tis with amazing difficulty I can help laughing.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Insolent vixen,
I had indulged a hope, madam, that the generosity and disinterested love I have evinced—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why as to your Lordship's generosity in condescending to marry a poor solitary spinster, I am certainly most duly grateful—and no one can possibly doubt your disinterestedness, who knows I am only heiress to 12,000l. a year—a fortune which, as I take it, nearly doubles the whole of your Lordship's rent roll!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Really, madam, if I am suspected of any mercenary motives, the liberal settlements which are now ready for your perusal, must immediately remove any such suspicion.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Oh, my Lord, you certainly mistake me —only as my papa observes, our estates do join so charmingly to one another!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Yes:—that circumstance is certainly advantageous to both parties.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Certainly!—only, as mine is the bigest, perhaps your's would be the greatest gainer by the bargain.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: My dear Madam, a title and the advantages of elevation in rank amply compensate the sacrifice on your part.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why, as to a title, my lord (as Mr. O'Dedimus, your attorney observes), there's no title in my mind better than a good title to a fine estate —and I see plainly, that altho' your lordship is a peer of the realm—you think this title of mine no mean companion for your own.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Nay, Madam—Believe me—I protest —I assure you—solemnly, that those considerations have very little—indeed no influence at all with me.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Oh, no!—only it is natural that you should feel (as papa again observes) that the contiguity of these estates seems to invite a union by a marriage between us.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: And if you admit that fact—why do you decline the invitation?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why, one doesn't accept every invitation that's offered, you know—one sometimes have very disagreeable ones; and then one presents compliments, and is extremely sorry that a previous engagement obliges us to decline the honour.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Confound the satirical hussey— But should not the wishes of your parents have some weight in the scale?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why, so they have; their wishes are in one scale, and mine are in the other; do all I can, I can't make mine weigh most, and so the beam remains balanced.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I should be sorry to make theirs preponderate, by calling in their authority as auxiliaries to their wishes.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Authority!—Ho! what, you think to marry me by force! do ye my Lord?

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: They are resolute—and if you continue obstinate—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I dare say your lordship's education hasn't precluded your knowledge of a very true, tho' rather vulgar proverb—“one man may lead a horse to the water, but twenty can't make him drink.”

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: The allusion may be classical, Madam, tho' certainly it is not very elegant—nor has it even the advantage of being applicable to the point in question. However, I do not despair to see this resolution changed. In the mean time, I did not think it in your nature to treat any man who loves you with cruelty and scorn.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Then, why don't you desist, my lord? If you'd take an answer, you had a civil one; but if you will follow and teaze one, like a sturdy beggar in the street, you must expect at last a reproof for your impertinence.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Yet even in their case perseverance often obtains what was denied to poverty.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Yes, possibly, from the feeble or the vain—But genuine Charity, and her sister, Love, act only from their own generous impulse, and scorn intimidation.

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: Are you alone, Madam?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No; I was only wishing to be so.

sp.speaker: Tiff.
sp.p: A young woman is without enquiring for Sir Willoughby, Ma'am; I thought he had been here.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Do you know her?

sp.speaker: Tiff.
sp.p: Yes, Ma'am; 'tis Fanny, the daughter of the odd man that lives on the common.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I'll see her my self—desire her to walk up.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Indeed! what brings her here?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why, what can be the matter now, your Lordship seems quite melancholy on a sudden.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I, madam! oh no!—or if I am—'tis merely a head ache—or some such cause—or perhaps owing to the influence of the weather.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Your Lordship is a very susceptible barometer —when you entered this room your countenance was set fair—but now I see the index points to stormy.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Madam, you have company, or business —a good morning to you.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Stay, stay, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Excuse me at present, I have an important affair—another time.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Surely, my Lord, the arrival of this innocent girl does not drive you away?

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Bless me, madam, what an idea! certainly not—but I have just recollected an engagement of consequence—some other time—Madam, your most obedient—

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: I beg pardon, madam, I'm fearful I intrude —but I enquired for Sir Willougby, and they shewed me to this room—I wished to speak with him on particular business—your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Pray stay, my good girl—I rejoice in this opportunity of becoming acquainted with you— the character I have heard of you has excited an affectionate interest—you must allow me to become your friend.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Indeed, indeed, madam, I am in want of friends—but you can never be one of them.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No! Why so?

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: You, madam! Oh no—you are the only enemy I ever had.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Enemy!—This is very extraordinary! I have scarce ever seen you before—Assuredly I never injured you.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Heaven forbid I should wish any one to injure you as deeply.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I cannot understand you—pray explain yourself.

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: That's impossible, madam—my Lord would never forgive me.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Your Lord! Let me entreat you to explain your meaning.

sp.speaker: Fan.
sp.p: I cannot, Madam; I came hither on business of importance, and no trifling business should have brought me to a house inhabited by one who is the cause of all my wretchedness.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: This is a most extraordinary affair! There is a mixture of cultivation and simplicity in your manner that affects me strongly—I see, my poor girl, you are distressed; and though what you have said leaves on my mind a painful suspicion—

sp.speaker: Fan:
sp.p: Oh heavens, Madam! stay, I beseech you! —I am not what you think me, indeed I am not— I must not, for a moment, let you think of me so injuriously—Yet I have promised secrecy!—but sure no promise can be binding, when to keep it we must sacrifice all that is valuable in life—Hear me then Madam—The struggle is violent, but I owe it to myself to acknowledge all.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: No, no, my dear girl! I now see what it would cost you to reveal your secret, and I will not listen to it—rest assured, I have no longer a thought to your disadvantage: Curiosity gives place to interest, for tho' 'tis cruelty to inflict a wound, 'tis still more deliberate barbarity to probe when we cannot hope to heal it.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Stay, madam, stay—your generosity overpowers me! oh madam!—you know not how wretched I am.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: What is it affects you thus?—come, if your story is of a nature that may be revealed, you are sure of sympathy.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: I never should have doubted; but my father has alarmed me sadly—he says my Lord Austencourt is certainly on the point of marriage with you.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And how, my dear girl, if it were so, could that affect you—come, you must be explicit.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Affect me! merciful heaven! can I see him wed another? He is my husband by every tie sacred and human.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Suffering, but too credulous girl! have you then trusted to his vows?

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: How madam! was I to blame—loving as I did—to trust in vows so solemn: could I suppose he would dare to break them, because our marriage was performed in secret!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Your marriage child! good heavens, you amaze me! but here we may be interrupted—this way with me—If this indeed be so, all may be well again; for tho' he may be dead to feeling be assured he is alive to fear: the man who once descends to be a villain is generally observed to be, at heart, a coward.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: The door of a Country Inn.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I've heard that intense thinking has driven some philosopher's mad!—now if this should happen to me, 'twill never be the fate of my young patron, Mr. Charles Austencourt, whom I have suddenly met on his sudden return from sea, and who never thinks at all—Poor gentleman, he little thinks what—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Not gone yet? How comes it you are not on the road to my father? Is the fellow deaf or dumb. Ponder! are ye asleep?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I'm thinking, whether I am or not.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: And what wise scheme occupies your thoughts?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Sir, I confess the subject is beneath me.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: The weight of the portmanteau, I suppose, alarms you.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: If that was my heaviest misfortune, Sir, I could carry double with all my heart—No, Sir— I was thinking that as your father, Sir Rowland, sent you on a cruise for some cause best known to himself; and as you have thought proper to return for some cause best known to yourself, the chances of war (if I may be allowed the expression) are, that the contents of that trunk will be your only inheritance—or in other words, that your father will cut you off with a shilling—and now I'm thinking—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No doubt—thinking takes up so many of your waking hours, that you seldom find time for doing. And so you have since my departure turned your thinking faculties to the law.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; when you gave me notice to quit, I found it so hard to live honestly, that lest the law should take to me, I took to the law; and so articled myself to Mr. O'Dedimus, the attorney in our town: but there is a thought unconnected with law that has occupied my head every moment since we met.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Pr'ythee dismiss your thoughts, and get your legs in motion.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Then, Sir, I have really been thinking, ever since I saw you, that you are a little—
a little odd hereabouts, Sir?
a little damned mad, if I may be allowed the expression!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Ha! ha! very probably! my sudden return, without a motive, as you suppose, has put that wise notion in your head.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Without a motive! No, Sir, I believe I know tolerably well the motive. The old story, Sir—Ha!—Love!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Love? And pray, sirrah, how do you dare to presume to suppose, that I—that I can be guilty of such a folly—I should be glad to know how you dare venture to think that I—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Lord bless you, Sir, I discovered it before you left the country.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Indeed! and by what symptoms, pray?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: The old symptoms, Sir—In the first place, frequent fits of my complaint.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Your complaint!

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes—thinking!—long reveries—sudden starts—sentimental sighs—fits of unobserving absence—fidgets and fevers—orders and counter-orders —loss of memory—loss of appetite—loss of rest, and loss of your senses, if I may be allowed the expression.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No, Sir—you may not be allowed the expression—'tis impertinent, 'tis false.—I never was unobserving or absent—I never had the fidgets —I never once mentioned the name of my adored Helen;—and, heigho! I never sighed for her in my life!

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Nor I, Sir; tho' I've been married these three years, I never once sighed for my dear wife in all that time—heigho!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I mustn't be angry with the fellow.— Why, I took you for an unobserving blockhead, or I would never have trusted you so near me.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Then, Sir, you mis-took me—I fancy it was in one of your most decided unobserving fits that you took me for a blockhead.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Well, Sir—I see you have discovered my secret; act wisely, and it may be of service to you.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Sir—I haven't studied the law for nothing. I'm no fool, if I may be allowed the expression.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I begin to suspect you have penetration enough to be useful to me.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: And craving your pardon, Sir, I begin to suspect your want of that faculty, from your not having found out that before.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I will now trust you, although once my servant, with the state of my heart.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Sir, that's very kind of you to trust your humble servant with a secret he had himself discovered ten months ago.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Keep it with honour and prudence.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Sir, I have kept it—nobody knows of it that I know of, except a few of your friends— many of your enemies—most travelling strangers, and all your neighbours.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Why, Zounds!—you don't mean to say that any body, except yourself, suspects me to be in love.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Suspects! no Sir!—Suspicion is out of the question; it is taken as a proved fact in all society—a bill found by every grand jury in the county.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: —The devil it is!—Zounds!—I shall never be able to shew my face—this will never do —my boasted disdain of ever bowing to the power of love—How ridiculous will it now render me— While the mystery and sacred secrecy of this attachment constituted the chief delight it gave to the refinement of my feelings—O! I'll off to sea again!—I won't stay here—Order a post-chaise— No—Yes—A chaise-and-four—d'ye hear?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes, Sir—but I'm thinking—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: That it is possible you may alter your mind.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No such thing, Sir—I'll set off this moment—order the chaise, I say—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Think of it again, Sir.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Will you obey my orders, or not?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I think I will.

Poor gentleman —now could I blow him up into a blaze in a minute, by telling that his mistress is just on the point of marriage with his cousin, but tho' they say “ill news travels apace,” they shall never say that I rode postillion on the occasion.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Here's a discovery!—all my delicate management destroy'd—known all over the country —I'm off! and yet to have travelled so far, and not to have one glympse of her! but then to be pointed at as a poor devil in love—a silly inconsistent boaster—no, that won't do—but then I may see her—yes—I'll see her once—just once— for three minutes—or three minutes and a half at most—no longer, positively—Ponder, Ponder!
Ponder, I say—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I wish you wou'dn't interrupt me, for —I'm thinking—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Damn your thinking, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I was only thinking that you may have alter'd your mind already.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I have not alter'd my mind. But since I am here, I should be wanting in duty not to pay my respects to my father; so march on with the trunk Sir.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes Sir—but if that's all you want to do Sir, you may spare yourself the trouble of going further, for most fortunately here he comes, and your noble cousin Lord Austencourt with him—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: The Devil!—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Yes Sir—the Devil—and his uncle, your father, if I may be allowed the expression.

div.stage: Enter Sir Rowland and Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: My dear father, I am heartily glad to see you—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: How is this—Charles! Returned thus unexpectedly?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Unexpected pleasure they say Sir, is always most welcome—I hope you find it so.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: This conduct youngster, requires explanation.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Sir, I have it ready at my tongue's end. My Lord, I ask your pardon—I'm glad to see you too—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I wish, Sir, I could return the compliment; but this extraordinary conduct—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No apologies my Lord, for your civil speech—you might easily have returned the compliment in the same words, and, believe me, with as much sincerity as it was offered.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: This is no time for dissention, Sir—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: My cousin forgets, Sir Rowland, that altho' united by ties of consanguinity, birth and fortune have placed me in a station which commands some respect,

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No my Lord, for I also am in a station where I too command respect—where I respect and am respected. I therefore well know what is due to my superiors; and this duty I never forget, till those above me forget what they owe to themselves.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I am not aware, good cousin, that I have ever yet forfeited my title to the respect I claim.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: You have, my lord; for high rank forfeits every claim to distinction when it exacts submissive humility from those beneath it, while at the same time it refuses a graceful condescension in exchange.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Charles, Charles, these sentiments but ill become the dependant state in which fortune has placed you.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Dependant state! Dependant upon whom?—What, on him—my titled, tawdry cousin there? What are his pretensions that he shall presume to brand me as a poor dependant?—What are his claims to independence?—How does he spend the income fortune has allotted to him? Does he rejoice to revive in the mansion of his ancestors the spirit of old English hospitality—do the eyes of aged tenants twinkle with joy when they hope his coming—do the poor bless his arrival? —I say no—He is the lord of land—and is also, what he seems still more proud of, a lord of parliament—but I will front him in both capacities, and frankly tell him, that in the first he is a burthen to his own estate, and not a benefactor— and in the second, a peer, but not a prop.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Charles, how dare you thus persevere— You cannot deny, rash and foolish boy, that you are in a dependant state—Your very profession proves it.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: O, Father, spare that insult—the profession I glory to belong to, is above dependence —Yes! while we live and fight, we feel, and gratefully acknowledge, that our pay depends on our king and country, and therefore you may style us dependent—but, in the hour of battle, we wish for nothing more than to show that the glory and safety of the nation depends on us—and by our death or blood to repay all previous obligation.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Dismiss this subject.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: With all my heart—My cousin was the subject, and he's a fatiguing one.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Tho' you do not love your cousin, you ought to pay that deference to his rank, which you refuse to his person.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Sir, I do—like a fine mansion in the hands of a bad inhabitant—I admire the building, but despise the tenant.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: This insolence is intolerable, and will not be forgotten!—You may find, hot Sir, that where my friendship is despised, my resentment may be feared. I well know the latent motives for this insult—it is the language of a losing gamester, and is treated with deserved contempt by a successful rival.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Ha! a successful rival!—is this possible?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: It is—the treaty of marriage between Lord Austencourt and Helen is this morning concluded.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: And does she consent?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: There can be little doubt of that.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: But little doubt! False Helen!— Come! Come! I know my Helen better.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I repeat my words, Sir—It is not the curse of every parent to have a disobedient child.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: By heaven, Sir, that reflection cuts me to the heart—you have ever found in me the obedience, nay more, the affection of a son, 'till circumstance on circumstance convinced me, I no longer possessed the affection of a father.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Charles—we are too warm—I feel that I have in some degree merited your severe reproof— give me your hand—and to convince you that you undervalue my feelings towards you, I will now confess that I have been employed during your absence, in planning an arrangement which will place you above the malice of fortune—you know our neighbour Mrs. Richland—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: What the gay widow with a fat jointure? What of her?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: She will make not only a rich, but a good wife. I know she likes you—I'm sure of it.—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Likes me?—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I am convinced she does.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: But—what the devil—she doesn't mean to marry me surely—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: That will, I am convinced, depend upon yourself—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Will it?—then by the Lord, tho' I sincerely esteem her, I shall make my bow, and decline the honor at once. No, Sir—the heart is my aim, and all the gold I care for in the hand that gives it, is the modest ring that encompasses the finger, and marks that hand as mine for ever.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Thus I see another of my prospects blighted! undutiful, degenerate boy! your folly and obstinacy will punish themselves—answer me not—think of the proposal I have made you!— obey your father's will, or for ever I renounce you!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Whoo! here's a whirligig!—I've drifted on to a pleasant lee shore here! Helen betrothed to another!!—Impossible—Oh Helen! Helen! Zounds! I'm going to make a soliloquy! this will never do—no—I'll see Helen—upbraid her falsehood —drop one tear to her memory—regain my frigate—seek the enemy—fight like a true sailor— die like a Briton, and leave my character and memory to my friends—and my blessing and forgiveness to Helen.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: So! having executed my commission, let me think a little—
for certain I, and my master, are too precious rogues
I wonder whether or not we shall be discovered, as assistants in this sham marriage

If we are, we shall be either transported or hanged, I wonder which:—My lord's bribe, however, was convenient; and in all cases of conscience versus convenience, 'tis the general rule of practice to non-suit the plaintiff. Ha! who's here? The poor girl herself.
I pity her; but I've been bribed; so I must be honest.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Oh, Sir, I'm in sad distress—my father has discovered my intercourse with Lord Austencourt, and says, he is sure my Lord means to deny our marriage; but I have told him, as you and your master were present, I am sure you will both be ready to prove it, should my Lord act so basely.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I must mind my hits here, or shall get myself into a confounded scrape—ready to do what, did you say, ma'am? to prove your marriage?

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Yes—as you both were present—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Present! me! Lord bless me, what is it you mean? Marriage! prove! me! present!

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Why do you hesitate—come, come—you do but jest with me—you cannot have forgotten it—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Hey? why no! but I can't say I remember it—

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Sure, sure, you cannot have the barbarity to deny that you were a witness to the ceremony!

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I may be mistaken—I've a remarkably short memory—but to the best of my recollection, I certainly—

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Aye—you recollect it—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: I certainly never was present—

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Cruel—you were—indeed, indeed you were.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: But at one wedding in my life.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: And that was mine—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: No, that was mine.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Merciful heaven! I see my fate—it is disgrace and misery?

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Bless you, if I could remember it—but I can't—however I'll speak to my master about it; if he recollects it, I dare say I shall.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: I have then no hope—and the fate of the hapless Fanny is decided.

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: Ha! yonder I see comes my master and his lordship. I wonder what they are thinking of —they're coming this way—I think we had better retire.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Oh hide me, hide me! in any corner let me hide my head, from scorn, from misery, and most of all, from him—

sp.speaker: Ponder.
sp.p: You can't escape that way, so you must come this—they won't think of coming here.
Poor girl! I've a great mind to confess the whole affair. What shall I get by that? Nothing! oh! that's contrary to law!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Are you certain no one can overhear us?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: There's nobody can hear us except my ould house-keeper, and she's as deaf as St. Dunstan's clock strikers.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: There is no time to be lost. You must immediately repair to Fanny—tell her my affection is unabated—tell her I shall ever love her, and make her such pecuniary offers, as shall convince her of my esteem and affection; but we must meet no more.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: We are betrayed!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Och! 'tis only my old housekeeper

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Your housekeeper! I thought you told me she was deaf.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Yes—but she isn't dumb—divil a word can she hear for sartain, but she's apt to say a great many, and so we may proceed.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You will easily accomplish this business with Fanny.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I'm afraid not—to tell you the truth my lord, I don't like the job.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Indeed—and why Sir?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Somehow, when I see a poor girl with her pretty little eyes brim full of tears, which I think have no business to be there, I'm more apt to be busy in wiping them away, than in saying cruel things that will make them flow faster— you had better tell her all this yourself, my lord.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: That Sir, is impossible—if you decline it, I shall find some one less delicate.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: There's reason in that, and if you send another to her, he may not be quite so delicate, as you say; so I'll even undertake it myself.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: The poor girl disposed of—If the old fool her father, will be thus clamorous, we must not be nice as to the means of silencing him —Money, I suppose, is his object.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: May be not—If a rich man by accident disables a poor man from working, money may make him easy—but when his feelings are deliberately tortured, devil fly away with the mercenary miser, if he will take shining dirt as a compensation for cruelty.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I can dispense with moral reflections— It may serve your purpose elsewhere, but to me, who know your practice, your preaching is ridiculous —What is it you propose? If the fellow won't be satisfied by money he must be removed.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Faith, 'tis a new way, sure enough, to make reparation to the feelings of a father, after having seduced his daughter under the plea of a false marriage—performed by a sham priest, and a forged licence!

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Oh, heaven! let me pass—I must and will see him—
Oh, my lord! my lord! my husband!—
sp.stage: (she falls at his feet, he raises her).
sp.p: Surely my ears deceived me—you cannot, cannot, mean it—a false marriage! a pretended priest!— What is to become of me? In mercy, kill me! —Let me not live to see my broken-hearted father expire with grief and shame, or live to curse me! —Spare me but this, my lord, and I will love— forgive—will pray for you—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: This is a plot against me—You placed her there on purpose to surprise me in the moment of unguarded weakness.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: By St. Patrick, how she came there is a most mysterious mystery to Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Fanny, I intreat you, leave me.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Oh, do not send me from you! Can you, my lord, abandon thus to shame and wretchedness, the poor deluded victim of your treachery!

sp.speaker: Lord A,
sp.p: Ha! leave me, I charge you!

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: No, no, my dearest lord! I cannot leave you! Whither shall I fly, if these arms deny me refuge!—Am I not your's?—What if these wicked men refuse me justice! There is another witness who will rise in dreadful evidence against you! 'Tis heaven itself! 'Tis there your vows were heard! 'tis there, where truth resides, your vows are registered!—Then, oh! reflect before you plunge too deep in guilt for repentance and retreat —reflect, that we are married!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I cannot speak at present—leave me, and we will meet again.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Do not command me from you—I see your heart is softened by my tears—Cherish the stranger Pity, in your breast—'tis noble! excellent! Such pity, in itself, is virtue!—Oh, cherish it, my lord! nor let the selfish feelings of the world step in to smother it!—Now!—now, while it glows unstifled in your heart.—Now, ere it dies, to be revived no more—at once proclaim the triumph of your virtue, and receive into your arms a fond and an acknowledged wife!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Ha! impossible—Urge me no more! I cannot—will not hear you—My heart has ever been your own—my hand MUST be another's—still we may love each other—still we may sometimes meet.

sp.speaker: Fanny
sp.p: I understand you. No, Sir! Since it must be, we will meet no more! I know that there are laws—but to these laws I disdain to fly!—Mine is an injury that cannot be redressed, for the only mortal witnesses to our union you have suborned—the laws therefore cannot do me justice, and I will never—inhuman as you are—I will never seek them for revenge.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I'm thinking, that if I was a lord, I should act in a clean contrary way—By the powers now, that man has got what I call a tough constitution —his heart's made of stone, like a brick-wall —ah, that a man should have the power of a man, and not know how to behave like a man!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: What's to be done? speak—advise me!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's it—have you made up your mind already, that you ask me to advise you?

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I know not how to act.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: When a man's in doubt whether he should act as an honest man or a rogue, there are two or three small reasons for choosing the right side.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: What is't you mean, Sir—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I mean this thing—that as I suppose you're in doubt, whether to persecute the poor souls, or to marry the sweet girl in right earnest.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Marry her! I have no such thoughts— idiot!—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Ideot! That's no proof of your lordship's wisdom to come and ask advice of one. —Ideot, by St. Patrick!—an ideot's a fool, and that's a christian name was never sprinkled upon Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I can feel for the unfortunate girl as well as you, but the idea of marrying her is too ridiculous.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: The unfortunate girl never knew misfortune 'till she knew you, my lord—and I heartily wish your lordship may never look more ridiculous than you would do in performing an act of justice and mercy.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You presume strangely, Sir, on my confidence and condescension!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: The unfortunate girl never knew misfortune 'till she knew you, my lord—and I heartily wish your lordship may never look more ridiculous than you would do in performing an act of justice and mercy.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You presume strangely, Sir, on my confidence and condescension!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: What! Are you coming over me now with the pride of your condescension.—That for your condescension!—when a great man, my lord, does me the honor to confide in me, he'll find me trusty and respectful—but when he condescends to make me an agent and a partner in his iniquity, by your leave, from that moment there's an end of distinction between us.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: There's no enduring this!—Scoundrel!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Scoundrel! ditto, my lord, ditto! If I'm a scoundrel, it was you that made me one, and by St. Patrick, there's a brace of us.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: The fellow has me in his power at present—you see me irritated, and you ought to bear with me—let us think of this no more.— The father and daughter must both be provided for out of that money which Sir Rowland still holds in trust for me.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And if you depend upon that money to silence the old man, you might as well think to stop a mouse-hole with toasted cheese.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Pray explain, Sir.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Devil a penny of it is there left. Sir Rowland ventured it in a speculation, and all is lost—Oh! blister my tongue, I've let out the secret, sure enough—!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Indeed! and what right had Sir Rowland to risk my property—be assured I will exact every guinea of it.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's just what I told him. Sir, says I, his lordship is one of the flinty-hearted ones, and devil a thirteener will he forgive you—but, my lord, it will utterly ruin Sir Rowland to replace it.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Sir Rowland should have thought of that before he embarked my property in a hazardous enterprize. Inform him, Sir, from me, that I expect an instant account of it.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I shall do that thing, Sir. But please to reflect a little—the money, so laid out, was honestly intended for your advantage.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Another word, Sir, and I shall think it necessary to employ another attorney.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sir, that's a quietus—I've done—only remember—that if you proceed to extremities, I warrant you'll repent it.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You warrant—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, and a warrant of attorney is reckoned decent good security.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Since my uncle has so far forgotten his duty as a guardian, I have now an opportunity, which I shall not neglect, to bring him to a proper recollection—you have nothing to do but to obey my orders; and these are, that the fourteen thousand pounds, of which he has defrauded my estate, shall be immediately repaid—look to it, Sir, and to the other affair you are entrusted with, and see that the law neglects no measures to recover what is due to me.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And by St. Patrick, if the law gives you what is due to you—that's—what I'm too polite to mention—you've had your swing in iniquity long enough, and such swings are very apt to end in one that's much too exalted for my notions.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Sir Willoughby, and William meeting him, the latter delivers a letter.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: The gentleman desired me to say he is below, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Hey?

“My dear Worrett, I hope that a long absence from my native land has not obliterated the recollection of our friendship. I have thought it right to adopt this method of announcing my return, lest my too sudden appearance should hurt your feelings by deranging the delicate nerves of your—amiable —lady. Hey!“Ever your's, Frederick Falkner.”Bless my soul! Falkner alive—shew the gentleman up!

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: He's here, Sir.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: My old friend, I rejoice to see you.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Friend Falkner, I shan't attempt to say how welcome your return is—we all thought you dead and buried—where have you been all these years?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: A wanderer? Let that suffice.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I see you still retain your old antipathy to answering questions, so I shall ask none— Have you been in France or among the Savages? Hey? I remember you had a daughter at school— is she alive? Is she merry or miserable? Is she married?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Zounds what a medly! France and Savages! marriage and misery!—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Ods life I'm happy to see you! I hav'nt been so cheerful or happy for many a day.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: How's your wife?

sp.speaker: Sir. W.
sp.p: Hey! thankye, Sir! why that excellent, good, woman, is in high health—in astonishing health—by my troth I speak it with unspeakable joy, I think she's a better wife now than she was when I married her!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: That must be a source of vast comfort to you—I don't wonder at your being so cheerful and happy.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: True—but it is'nt that—that is, not altogether so—no—'tis that I once more hold my friend Falkner by the hand, and that my daughter—you remember your little favourite Helen—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: I do indeed!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: You are arrived at a critical moment —I mean shortly to marry her—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: I forbid the banns!—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: The devil you do!

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Pshaw!
my feelings o'erstep my discretion. Take care what you're about —If you're an honest man, you'd rather see her dead than married to a villain—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: To be sure I would—but the man I mean her to marry—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Perhaps will never be her husband.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: The devil he wont!—why not?

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Talk of something else—you know I was always an eccentric being—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: What the devil does he mean?—yes, yes, you was always eccentric—but do you know—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: I know more than I wish to know; I've lived long enough in the world to know that roguery fattens on the same soil where honesty starves; and I care little whether time adds to information which opens to me more and more the depravity of human nature.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why, Falkner, you are grown more a misanthrope than ever.

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: You know well enough I have had my vexations in life—in an early stage of it I married—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Every man has his trials!—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: About two years afterwards, I lost my wife.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That was a heavy misfortune! however you bore it with fortitude.

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: I bore it easy. My wife was a woman without feelings—she had not energy for great virtue, and she had no vice, because she had no passion—life with her was a state of stagnation.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: How different are the fates of men!

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: In the next instance I had a friend whom I would have trusted with my life—with more—my honour—I need not tell you then I thought him the first of human beings—but I was mistaken—he understood my character no better than I knew his—he confided to me a transaction which proved him to be a villain, and I commanded him never to see me more.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Bless me! what was that transaction?

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: It was a secret, and has remained so. Tho' I should have liked to hang the fellow, he had trusted me, and no living creature but himself and me at this day is possessed of it.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Strange indeed; and what became of him?

sp.speaker: Falkner,
sp.p: I have not seen him since, but I shall see him in a few hours.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Indeed, is he in this neighbourhood?

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: That circumstance of my friend, and a loss in the West Indies, which shook the fabric of my fortune to its foundation, drove me from the world—I am now returned to it with better prospects—my property which I then thought lost is doubled—circumstances have called me hither on an important errand, and before we are four and twenty hours older, you may see some changes which will make you doubt your own senses for the remainder of your days—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: You astonish me mightily.

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Yes—you stare as if you were astonished: but why do I stay chattering here?— I must be gone.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Nay, prythee now—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Pshaw!—I have paid my first visit to you, because you are the first in my esteem —don't weaken it by awkward and unseasonable ceremony—I must now about the business that brings me here—no interruption—if you wish to see me again let me have my own way, and I may, perhaps, be back in half an hour.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: But I want to tell you that—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: I know—I know—you want to prove to me that you're the least talker, and the best husband in the county; but both secrets must keep till my return, when I shall be happy to congratulate you—and so farewell—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Bless my soul what can he mean?— “I forbid the banns—lost my wife—horrid transaction —back again in half an hour”—dear me— John—Thomas! Lady Worrett! Helen!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: —A Room in Sir Willoughby Worrett's house. Helen and Charles meeting— Helen screams—they run towards each other as if to embrace—Charles stops suddenly.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Charles! is it you, or is it your spirit?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: 'Tis I, madam, and you'll find I have brought my spirit with me.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Hey! why what the deuce ails the man?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: My presence here no doubt astonishes you.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Yes, sir, your presence does astonish me, but your manner still more.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I understand you—you would still keep a poor devil in your toils, tho' in his absence you have been sporting with nobler game.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: My good friend, will you descend from your heroical stilts, and explain your meaning in plain English?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: There needs no explanation of my conduct—call it caprice—say, if you please, that I am altered—say I have changed my mind, and love another better—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Indeed! and is it come to this! He shall not see he mortifies me however—
Since you are in this mind, sir, I wish you had been pleased to signify the same by letter, sir—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: By letter?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Yes, sir—for this personal visit being rather unexpected, does not promise to be particularly pleasant—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I believe so, madam—you did not calculate, I fancy, on this sudden return.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No indeed, sir—and should have shewn all Christian patience if this sudden return had'nt happened these twelve months.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: The devil you would! madam!—but I'll be cool—I'll cut her to the heart with a razor of ice—I'll congeal her with indifference —you must know, madam—

sp.speaker: Helen.
