sp.p: Bless me, Charles, how very strangely you look—you're pale and red, and red and pale, in the same moment! why you can scarcely breathe! and now you tremble so! I'am afraid you are very ill.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Sarcastic!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: You move all over like a ship in a storm!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Vastly well, madam—and now—

sp.speaker: Helen,
sp.p: Your teeth chatter!—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Fire and faggots, madam, I will speak.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Do, dear Charles, while you are able —your voice will be gone in a minute or two and then—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I will be heard!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: That you will indeed—and all over the house, too.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Madam, will you hear me or not?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I am glad to find there's no affection of the lungs!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Death and torments! may I be allowed to speak—yes, or no?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Yes, but gently, and make haste before they call the watch.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Madam, madam—I wish to keep my temper—I wish to be cool.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Perhaps this will answer the purpose

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Is she laughing at me now—or trying to wheedle me into a good humour?—I feel, Miss Worrett, that I am expressing myself with too much warmth—I must therefore inform you that being ordered home with dispatches, and having some leisure time on my hands on my return; I thought it but proper as I passed the house to call at your door—just to say—a—a—just civilly to say—false! cruel! perfidious girl! you may break the tough heart of a sailor, but damn me if he will ever own it broke for love of you!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: On my honor, sir, I do not understand what all this means.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: You don't?—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No, sir—if your purpose here is insult, you might, methinks, have found some fitter object than one who has so limited a power to resent it!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Stay, madam—stay—what a face is there! a smile upon it too—oh Helen—spare those smiles—they once could wake my soul to extacy; but now they rouze it into madness: save them, madam, for a happier lover—save them for Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Charles—Charles, you have been deceived. —but come—set down and hear me.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I am all attention, and listen to you with all that patience which the subject demands.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: As you know the world, Charles, you cannot wonder that my father, (in the main a very good father, but in this respect, like all other fathers) should wish to unite his daughter to a man whose rank and fortune—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Spare yourself the trouble of further explanation, madam; I see the whole at once—you are now going to tell me about prudence, duty, obedience, filial affection, and all the canting catalogue of fine phrases that serve to gloss over the giddy frailty of your sex, when you sacrifice the person and the heart at the frequented shrine of avarice and ambition!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: When I am next inclined to descend to explanation, sir, I hope you will be better disposed to attend to me.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: A moment, madam! The whole explanation lies in a word—has not your father concluded a treaty of marriage between you and Lord Austencourt?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: He has—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: There—'tis enough! you have confessed it—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Confess'd what? you monster! I've confessed nothing.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Haven't you acknowledged that you are to be the wife of another?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No.—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No! won't you consent then?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Half an hour ago nothing on earth should have induced me to consent—but since I see, Charles, of what your temper is capable, I shall think it more laudable to risk my happiness by obedience to my father, than by an ill-judged constancy to one who seems so little inclined to deserve it.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Hey? where am I? zounds! I see my whole error at once! oh, Helen, Helen—for mercy's sake one moment more?—She's gone—and has left me in anger!—but I will see her again, and obtain her forgiveness—fool, ideot, dolt, ass, that I am, to suffer my cursed temper to master reason and affection at the risk of losing the dearest blessing of life—a lovely and an amiable woman.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter Charles pulling in Ponder by the collar.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: This way, Sirrah, this way, and now out with your confession if you expect mercy at my hands.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: I will, Sir, I will—but I expect no mercy at your hands, for you've already handled me most unmercifully—
, what would you please to have me confess, sir?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I have seen old Abel Grouse—he has told me the story of his daughter's marriage with this amiable cousin of mine—now, sirrah, confess the truth—were you present—or were you not?—out with it.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Now pray recollect yourself—do, sir— think a little.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Recollect myself?—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Aye, sir—if you will but take time to reflect, you'll give me time to collect my scattered thoughts, which you have completely shaken out of my pericranium.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No equivocation, answer directly, or tho' you are no longer my servant, by heavens I'll—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Sir—for heaven's sake!—you'll shake nothing more out of me, depend on't—If you'll be pleased to pause a moment I'll think of an answer.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: It requires no recollection to say whether you were a witness—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: No indeed, sir—ask my master if I was— besides if I had been, my conscience would'nt let me disclose it.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Your conscience! good, and you're articled to an attorney!

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: True, sir—but there's a deal of conscience in our office—if my master knew I betrayed his secrets even to you, I believe (in conscience,) he'd hang me if he could.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: If my old friend O'Dedimus proves a rogue at last, I shan't wonder that you have followed his example.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: No, sir, for I always follow my master's example, even tho' it should be in the path of roguery—compliment apart sir, I always followed yours—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Puppy—you trifle with my patience.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: No indeed, sir, I never play with edg'd tools.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: You wont acknowledge it then.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Yes, sir, I'll acknowledge the truth, but I scorn a lie.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: 'Tis true I always thought you honest —I have ever trusted you, Ponder, even as a friend—I do not believe you capable of deceiving me.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Sir,
I can't swallow that! it choaks me
forgive me, dear master that was; your threats I could withstand —your violence I could bear, but your kindness and good opinion there is no resisting; promise you wont betray me—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: So; now it comes—I do—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Then, sir, the whole truth shall out— they are married, sir—and they are not married, sir—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Enigma too!

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Yes, sir—they are married—but the priest was ordained by my master, and the licence was of his own granting—and so they are not married, and now the enigma's explained—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Your master then is a villain!

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: I don't know, sir—that puzzles me—but he's such an honest fellow I can hardly think him a rogue—tho' I fancy, sir, between ourselves he's like the rest of the world—half and half—or like punch, sir, a mixture of opposites—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: So! villany has been thriving in my absence. If you feel the attachment you profess why did you not confide this to me before?

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Sir, truth to speak, I did not tell you, because, knowing the natural gentleness of your disposition, which I have so often admired—I was alarmed, lest the sudden shock should cause one of those irascible fits, which I have so often witnessed, and produce some of those shakes and buffets, which to my unspeakable astonishment, I have so often experienced.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: And which, I can tell you, you have now so narrowly escaped—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: True sir, I have escaped as narrowly as a felon who gets his reprieve five minutes after execution.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Something must be done—I am involved in a quarrel with Helen too!—curse on my irritable temper—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: So I say, sir—try and mend it—pray do—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I am resolved to have another interview with her;—to throw myself at her feet, and sue for pardon! Tho' fate should oppose our union, I may still preserve her from the arms of a villain, who is capable of deceiving the innocent he could not seduce; and of planting a dagger in the female heart, where nature has bestowed her softest attributes, and has only left it weak, that man might cherish, shelter, and protect it—

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: So! Now I'm a rogue both ways—If I escape punishment one way, I shall certainly meet it the other—But if my good luck saves me both ways I shall never more credit a fortune-teller— for one once predicted, that I was born to be hang'd.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: You have betrayed me then!—Did not I caution you to keep secret from my nephew this accursed loss.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And so you did sure enough—but somehow it slipt out before I said a word about it: but I told him it was a secret, and I dare say he wont mention it—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: But you say, that he demands the immediate liquidation—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Aye, sir, and has given me orders to proceed against you—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Is it possible—in a moment could I arrest his impious progress—but I will probe him to the quick—did he threaten me, say you?—There is however one way to save him from this public avowal of his baseness, and me from his intended persecution—a marriage between Charles and Mrs. Richland.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: The widow's as rich as the Wicklow mines!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: The boy refuses to comply with my wishes; we may find ways, however, to compel him—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: He's a sailor; and gentlemen of his kidney are generally pretty tough when they take a notion in their heads.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I am resolved to carry my point. I have reason to believe you advanced him a sum of money.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I did that thing—he's a brave fellow— I'd do that thing again—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: You did wrong, sir, to encourage a young spenthrift in disobedience to his father.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I did right, sir, to assist the son of a client, and the nephew of a benefactor, especially when his father had'nt the civility to do it.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Mr. O'Dedimus, you grow impertinent.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sir Rowland, I grow old; and 'tis one privilege of age to grow blunt. I advanced your son a sum of money, because I esteemed him.—I tack'd no usurious obligation to the bond he gave me, and I never came to ask you for security—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: You have his bond then—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I have, sir; his bond and judgement for two hundred pounds.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: It is enough—then you can indeed assist my views,—the dread of confinement will, no doubt, alter his resolutions, you must enter up judgment, and proceed on your bond—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: If I proceed upon my bond, it will be very much against my judgment—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: In order to alarm him, you must arrest him immediately—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sir Rowland, I wish to treat you with respect—but when without a blush on your cheek you ask me to make myself a rascal, I must either be a scoundrel ready-made to your hands, for respecting you, or a damn'd hypocrite for pretending to do it—I see you are angry, sir, and I can't help that; and so, having delivered my message, for fear I should say any thing uncivil or ungenteel, I wish you a most beautiful good morning.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Then I have but one way left—my fatal secret must be publicly revealed—oh horror! ruin irretrievable is preferable—never—never— that secret shall die with me.—
as 'tis probably already buried in the grave with Falkner.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: 'Tis false—'tis buried only in his heart!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Falkner!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: 'Tis eighteen years since last we met. You have not, I find, forgotten the theme on which we parted.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Oh, no! my heart's reproaches never would allow me! Oh Falkner—I and the world for many years have thought you numbered with the dead.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: To the world I was so—I have returned to it to do an act of justice.—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Will you then betray me?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: During eighteen years, sir, I have been the depositary of a secret, which, if it does not actually affect your life, affects what should be dearer than life, your honor.—If, in the moment that your ill-judged confidence avowed you as the man you are, and robbed me of that friendship which I held sacred as my being—If in that bitter moment I concealed my knowledge of your guilt from an imperious principle of honor, It is not likely, that the years which time has added to my life, should have taught me perfidy— your secret still is safe—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Oh, Falkner—you have snatched a load of misery from my heart—I breathe—I live again—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Your exultation flows from a polluted source—I return to the world to seek you—to warn and to expostulate—I come to urge you to brave the infamy you have deserved—to court disgrace as the punishment you merit— briefly to avow your guilty secret.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Name it not for mercy's sake! It is impossible! How shall I sustain the world's contempt —its scorn—revilings and reproaches—?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Can he, who has sustained so long the reproaches of his conscience, fear the world's revilings? —Oh Austencourt! Once you had a heart.—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Sir—it is callous now to every thing but shame, when it lost you, it's dearest only friend, its noblest feelings were extinguished—my crime has been my punishment, for it has brought on me, nothing but remorse and misery—still is my fame untainted by the world, and I will never court its contumely—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: You are determined—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I am!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Have you no fear from me?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: None! You have renewed your promise, and I am safe.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Nothing then remains for me but to return to that obscurity from whence I have emerged —had I found you barely leaning to the side of virtue, I had arguments to urge that might have fixed a wavering purpose, but I find you resolute —hardened and determined in guilt, and I leave you to your fate—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Stay, Falkner—there is a meaning in your words—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: A dreadful precipice lies before you, be wary how you tread! there is a being injured by your—by Lord Austencourt—see that he makes her reparation by an immediate marriage—look first to that—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: To such a degradation could I forget my noble ancestry, he never will consent.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Look next to yourself—he is not a half villain—and it is not the ties of consanguinity will save you from a jail. Beware how you proceed with Charles—you see I am acquainted with more than you suspected—look to it, sir, for the day is not yet passed that by restoring you to virtue, may restore to you a friend; or should you persevere in guilty silence, that may draw down unexpected vengeance on your head—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Mysterious man! a moment stay! I cannot live in this dreadful uncertainty! whatever is my fate, it shall be decided quickly.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: —An Apartment at Sir Willoughby's; a Door in the Flat.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I tell you, it is useless to follow me, sir. The proud spirit you evinced this morning, might have saved you methinks from this meanness of solicitation—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Surely now a frank acknowledgement of error deserves a milder epithet than meanness—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: As you seem equally disposed, sir, to quarrel with my words, as you are to question my conduct, I fear you will have little cause to congratulate yourself on this forced and tiresome interview—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Forced interview! Did ever woman so consider the anxiety of a lover to seek explanation and forgiveness!—Helen, Helen, you torture me—is this generous?—is it like yourself? surely if you lov'd me—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Charles—I do love you—that is—I did love you, but—I don't love you—but
ah! now I'm going to make bad worse—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: But what, Helen?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: The violence of temper you have discovered this morning, has shewn me the dark side of your character; it has given a pause to affection, and afforded me time to reflect—now tho' I do really and truly believe that—you—love me Charles.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I must see my daughter directly —where is she?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: Ma'am, ma'am, your father's coming up stairs, with a letter in his hand, muttering something about Mr. Charles; as sure as life you'll be discovered.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: For heav'n's sake hide yourself—I would not have him find you here for worlds—here, step into the music-room.—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Promise me first your forgiveness—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Charles, retire, I entreat you—make haste—he is here—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: On my knees—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Then kneel in the next room.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Give me but your hand—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: That is now at my own disposal—I beseech you go—
sp.stage: (Charles just gains the door when enters Sir Willoughby with a letter in his hand, and Lady Worrett—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Gadzooks! Here's a discovery!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: A discovery, sir?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Aye, a discovery indeed!—Odslife! I'm in a furious passion!—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Dear Sir—not with me I hope—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Let me entreat you Sir Willoughby to compose yourself—recollect that anger is very apt to bring on the gout.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Damn the gout—I must be in a passion —my—life—harkye, daughter—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: They know he's here! so I may as well own it at once.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Pray compose yourself, remember we have no proof.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why that's true—that is remarkably true—I must compose myself—I will—I do—I am composed—and now let me open the affair with coolness and deliberation! Daughter, come hither.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Yes, sir—now for it!—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Daughter, you are in general, a very good, dutiful, and obedient child—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I know it, papa—and was from a child, and I always will be.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Allow me, Sir Willoughby—you are in general a child, a very headstrong, disobedient, and undutiful daughter.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I know it, mamma—and was from a child, and always will be.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: How, madam!—Remember, Sir Willoughby —there is a proper medium between too violent a severity, and too gentle a lenity.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Zounds, madam, in your own curs'd economy there is no medium—but don't bawl so, or we shall be overheard—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Sir Willoughby, you are very ill I'm sure—but I must now attend to this business— daughter, we have heard that Charles—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Lady Worrett, my—love—let me speak —you know, child, it is the duty of an obedient daughter, to obey her parents.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I know it, papa—and when I obey you, I am, generally, obedient.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: In short, child, I say again,—we learn that Charles—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Lady Worrett, Lady Worrett, you are too abrupt—od-rabbit it, madam, I will be heard—this affair concerns the honor of my family, and on this one occasion, I will be my own spokesman.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Oh heavens! Your violence affects my brain.

sp.speaker: Sir. W.
sp.p: Does it? I wish it would affect your tongue, with all my heart—bless my soul, what have I said! Lady Worrett! Lady Worrett! you drive me out of my senses, and then wonder that I act like a madman—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Barbarous man—your cruelty will break my heart, and I shall leave you, Sir Willoughby, to deplore my loss, in unavailing despair, and everlasting anguish.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I am afraid not—such despair and anguish will never be my—happy—lot!— bless me how quiet the room is—what can be— oh my wife's gone!—now then we may proceed to business—and so daughter, this young fellow, Charles, has dared to return in direct disobedience to his father's commands.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I had better confess it all at once—he has, he has—my dear papa, I do confess, it was very, very wrong—but pray now do forgive—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I—forgive him—never—nor his father will never forgive him, Sir Rowland writes me here, to take care of you, I have before given him my solemn promise to prevent your meeting, and I am sorry to say, I hav'nt the least doubt that you know he is here, and will—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I do confess, he is here papa—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, you'll confess it fast enough, now I've found it out—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Indeed I was so afraid you would find it out, that I—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Find it out!—his father writes me word, he has been here in the village these three hours!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: In the village!—Oh, what you heard he was in the village?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, and being afraid he should find his way to my house, egad I never was brisker after the fox-hounds, than I was after you, in fear of finding you at a fault, you puss—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Oh! you were afraid he should come here, were you?—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, but I'll take care he shan't, however —as my maxim is (now my wife doesn't hear me), to trust your sex no farther than I can possibly help—I shall just put you, my dear child, under lock and key, 'till this young son of the ocean, is bundled off to sea again.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: What! lock me up?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Damme if I dont—come walk into that room, and I'll take the key with me.
sp.stage: (Pointing to the room where Charles entered).

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Into that room?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And do you think I shall stay there by myself?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No, no—here Tiffany
—Miss Pert, here, shall keep you company —I'll have no whisperings thro' key-holes, nor letters thrust under doors.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And you'll really lock me up in that room?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Upon my soul I will.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Now dear papa, be persuaded—take my advice, and don't—

sp.speaker: Sir. W.
sp.p: If I don't, I wish you may be in Charles Austencourt's arms in three minutes from this present speaking.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And if you do,—take my word for it I might be in his arms if I chose, in less than two minutes from this present warning.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Might you so? Ha! ha! I'll give you leave if you can—for unless you jump into them out of the window, I'll defy the devil and all his imps to bring you together.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: We shall come together without their assistance depend on it, papa.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Very well—and now, my dear, walk in.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: With all my heart, only remember you had better not.—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's a good girl—and you, you baggage, in with you

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: “Safe bind, safe find,” is one of my lady Worrett's favourite proverbs; and that's the only reason why I in general dislike it.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Once more welcome, my dear Falkner. What brings you back so soon?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: You have a daughter—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Well, I know I have.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: And a wife—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I'm much obliged to you for the information —You have been a widower some years I believe.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: What of that, do you envy me?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Envy you, what, because you are a widower? Eh! Zounds, I believe he is laughing at me

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: I am just informed that every thing is finally arranged between your lady and his lordship respecting Helen's marriage.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, every thing is happily settled.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: I am sincerely sorry to hear it.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: You are! I should have thought Mr. Falkner, that my daughter's happiness was dear to you.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: It is, and therefore I do not wish to see her married to Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why then what the devil is it you mean?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: To see her married to the man of her heart, with whom I trust to see her as happy—as you are with Lady Worrett.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, ha! ha! ha! yes! but you are in jest respecting my daughter.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: No matter! where is Helen?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Safe under lock and key.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Under lock and key!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Aye, in that very room—I've lock'd her up to keep her from that hot-headed young rogue Charles Austencourt—should you like to see her? she's grown a fine young woman!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: With all my heart!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: You'll be surprised, I can tell you—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: I dare say—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: We'll pop in upon her when she least expects it—I'll bet my life you'll be astonished at her appearance.

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Well, I shall be glad to see your daughter —but she must not marry this Lord.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No! who then?

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: The man she loves—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Hey! Oh yes! but who do you mean? Charles Austencourt?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Charles Austencourt!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.stage: (Aloud and striking the floor with his stick)
sp.p: Aye.—Charles Austencourt.—

sp.speaker: Charles,
sp.p: Here am I who calls?

div.stage: [Helen and Tiffany come forward and Tiffany goes off.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Fire and faggots! what do I see—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Ah! heavens defend me what do I behold!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Why is this the surprise you promised me? the astonishment seems general. Pray, Sir Willoughby, explain this puppet show!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Aye! pray Sir Willoughby explain—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Curse me if I can.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I told you how it would be, papa, and you would not believe me!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: So! pray, sir, condescend to inform Lady Worrett and me, how you introduced yourself into that most extraordinary situation.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Sir, I shall make no mystery of it, nor attempt to screen you from her Ladyship's just reproaches, by concealing one atom of the truth. The fact is, madam, that Sir Willoughby not only in my hearing, gave Miss Helen his unrestricted permission to throw herself into my arms, but actually forced her into the room where I was quietly seated, and positively and deliberately lock'd us in together!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Oh! I shall expire!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I've heard of matchless impudence, but curse me if this isn't the paragon of the species! Zounds! I'm in a wonderful passion! Daughter, I am resolved to have this affair explained to my satisfaction.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: You may have it explained, papa, but I fear it won't be to your satisfaction.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No, sir—nor to her Ladyship's either— and now, as my situation here is not remarkably agreeable I take my leave—madam, your most obedient—and Sir Willoughby, the next time you propose an agreeable surprise for your friends—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Harkye sir—how you came into my house I can't tell—but if you don't presently walk out of it—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I say—I heartily hope that you may accomplish your purpose—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Zounds, sir, leave my house—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Without finding yourself the most astonished of the party!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Thank heaven my house is rid of him.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: As usual, Sir Willoughby, a precious business you've made of this!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Death and furies, my Lady Worrett—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Gently, my old friend, gently—I'm one too many here during these little domestic discussions —but before I go, on two points let me caution you; let your daughter choose her own husband if you wish her to have one without leaping out of window to get at him; and be master of your own house and your own wife if you do not wish to continue, what you now are, the laughing-stock of all your acquaintance.—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Ah! the barbarian!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I'm thunderstruck —
sp.stage: (makes signs to Helen to go before.)

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Won't you go first, papa?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Hey? If I lose sight of you till you've explained this business, may I be laid up with the gout while you are galloping to Gretna Green! “Be master of your house and wife if you don't wish to continue, what you now are!—Hey? the laughing-stock of all your acquaintance! Sir Willoughby Worrett the laughing-stock of all his acquaintance! I think I see myself the laughing-stock of all my acquaintance!—
I'll follow you ladies! I'll reform! 'tis never too late to mend!

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: An Apartment at Sir Willoughby Worrett's.
Enter Sir Willoughby and Lady Worrett.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Lady Worrett! Lady Worrett! I will have a reform. I am at last resolved to be master of my own house, and so let us come to a right understanding, and I dare say we shall be the better friends for it in future.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: You shall see, Sir Willoughby, that I can change as suddenly as yourself. Though you have seen my delicate system deranged on slight occasions, you will find that in essential ones I have still spirit for resentment.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: I'll have my house in future conducted as a gentleman's should be, and I will no longer suffer my wife to make herself the object of ridicule to all her servants. So I'll give up the folly of wishing to be thought a tender husband, for the real honour of being found a respectable one. I'll make a glorious bonfire of all your musty collection of family receipt-books! and when I deliver up your keys to an honest housekeeper, I'll keep one back of a snug apartment in which to deposit a rebellious wife.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: That will be indeed the way to make yourself respectable. I have found means to manage you for some years, and it will be my own fault if I don't do so still.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Surely I dream! what? have you managed me? Hey? Zounds! I never suspected that. Has Sir Willoughby Worrett been lead in leading-strings all this time? Death and forty devils, Madam, have you presumed to manage me?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Yes, Sir; but you had better be silent on the subject, unless you mean to expose yourself to your daughter and all the world.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Aye, Madam, with all my heart; my daughter and all the world shall know it.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Here's a pretty piece of work!—what's the matter now, I wonder?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: How dare you overhear our domestic dissentions. What business have you to know we were quarrelling, Madam?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Lord love you! if I had heard it, I should not have listened—for its nothing new, you know, when you're alone; though you both look so loving in public.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's true—that is lamentably true— but all the world shall know it—I'll proclaim it— I'll print it—I'll advertize it!—She has usurped my rights and my power; and her fate, as every usurper's should be, shall be public downfall and disgrace.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: What, papa! and won't you let mamma-in-law rule the roast any longer?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No!—I am resolved from this moment no longer to give way to her absurd whims and wishes.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: You are!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Absolutely and immoveably.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And you will venture to contradict her?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: On every occasion—right or wrong.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: That's right—Pray, Madam, don't you wish me to marry Lord Austencourt?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: You know my will on that head, Miss Helen.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Then, papa, of course you wish me to marry Charles Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: What! no such thing—no such thing —what! marry a beggar?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: But you won't let Mama rule the roast, will you, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: 'Tis a great match! I believe in that one point we shall still agree—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: You may spare your persuasions, Madam, and leave the room—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: What—my daughter leave the room? Stay here, Helen.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: To be sure I shall—I eame on purpose to tell you the news! oh, tis a pretty piece of work!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: What does the girl mean?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Why, I mean that in order to ruin a poor innocent girl, in our neighbourhood, this amiable Lord has prevailed on her to consent to a private marriage—and it now comes out that it was all a mock marriage, performed by a sham priest, and a false license!

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: I don't believe one word of it.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: But I do—and shall inquire into it immediately.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Such a match for your daughter is not to be relinquished on slight grounds; and though his Lordship should have been guilty of some indiscretion, it will not alter my resolution respecting his union with Helen.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No—but it will mine—and to prove to you, Madam, that however you may rule your household, you shall no longer rule me—if the story has any foundation—I say—she shall not marry Lord Austencourt.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Shall not?

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: No, Madam, shall not—and so ends your management, and thus begins my career of new-born authority. I'm out of leading-strings now, and Madam, I'll manage you, dam'me if I do not.

sp.speaker: Helen
sp.p: You hear papa's will on that head, Ma'am.

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: I hear nothing!—I see nothing!—I shall go mad with vexation and disappointment, and if I do not break his resolution, I am determined to break his heart; and my own heart, and your heart, and the hearts of all the rest of the family.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: There she goes, with a laudable matrimonial resolution. Heigho! with such an example before my eyes, I believe I shall never have resolution to die an old maid. Oh, Charles, Charles —why did you take me at my word?—Bless me! sure I saw him then—'tis he indeed! So, my gentleman, are you there? I'll just retire and watch his motions a little

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: What a pretty state am I reduced to? though I am resolved to speak with this ungrateful girl but once more before I leave her for ever, here am I, skulking under the enemy's batteries as though I was afraid of an encounter!—Yes, I'll see her, upbraid her, and then leave her for ever! heigho! she's a false, deceitful—dear, bewitching girl, and—however, I am resolved that nothing on earth—not even her tears, shall now induce me to forgive her.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Ha!—hark ye, young woman! pray are the family at home?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: My lady is at home, Sir—would you please to see her?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Your lady—do you mean your young lady?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: No, Sir, I mean my lady.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: What, your old lady?—No—I don't wish to see her. Are all the rest of the family from home—

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: No, Sir—Sir Willoughby is within— I'll tell him you are here,

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: By no means—stay—stay! what then, they are all at home except Miss Helen.

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: She's at home too, Sir—but I suppose she don't wish to see you.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: You suppose!

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: I'm sure she's been in a monstrous ill-humour ever since you came back, Sir—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: The devil she has!—and pray now are you of opinion that my return is the cause of her ill-humour?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: Lord, Sir—what interest have I in knowing such things?—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Interest!—oh, ho! the old story! why hark ye, my dear—your mistress has a lord for her lover, so I suppose he has secured a warmer interest than I can afford to purchase—however, I know the custom, and thus I comply with it, in hopes you will tell me whether you really think my return has caused your young mistress' ill-humour—

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: A guinea! well! I declare! why really, Sir—when I say Miss Helen has been out of humour on your account, I don't mean to say it is on account of your return, but on account of your going away again—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No! my dear Tiffany.

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: And I am sure I don't wonder at her being cross about it, for if I was my mistress I never would listen with patience (any more than she does) to such a disagreeable creature as my lord, while such a generous nice gentleman as you was ready to make love to me.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: You couldn't?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: No, Sir—and I'm sure she's quite altered and melancholy gone since you quarrelled with her, and she vows now more than ever that she never will consent to marry my lord, or any body but you—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: My dear Tiffany!—let me catch the sounds from your rosy lips.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Bless me! I am afraid I interrupt business here!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I—I—I—Upon my soul, Madam— what you saw was—

sp.speaker: Tiff.
sp.p: Ye—ye—yes—upon my word, Ma'am— what you saw was.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: What I saw was very clear indeed!—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Hear me but explain—you do not understand.—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: I rather think I do understand—

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: Indeed, Ma'am, Mr. Charles was only whispering something I was to tell you—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And pray, Ma'am, do you suffer gentlemen in general to whisper in that fashion?—what do you stand stammering and blushing there for? —why don't you go?

sp.speaker: Tiffany.
sp.p: Yes, Ma'am,—but I assure you—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: What! you stay to be whispered to again, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Let me explain this,—oh, Helen—can you be surprised?—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No, Sir, I can't be surprised at any thing after what I have just witnessed—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: On my soul, it was excess of joy at hearing you still lov'd me, that led me into this confounded scrape.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Sir, you should not believe it—I don't love you. I wont love you,—and after what I have just seen, you can't expect I should love you—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Helen! Helen! you make no allowance for the fears of a man who loves you to distraction. I have borne a great deal, and can bear but very little more—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Poor man! you're sadly loaded with grievances, to be sure; and by and by, I suppose, like a horse or a mule, or some such stubborn animal, having more than you can bear, you'll kick a little, and plunge a little, and then down on your knees again!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: I gloried even in that humble posture, while you taught me to believe you lov'd me.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Tis true, my heart was once your own, but I never can, nor ought to forgive you—for thinking me capable of being unfaithful to you.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Dearest dear Helen! and has your anger then no other cause? surely you could not blame a resentment which was the offspring of my fond affection?

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: No! to be sure I couldn't, who could! —but what should I not have to dread from the violence of your temper, if I consented—to run away with you?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Run away with me!—no!—zounds I've a chaise in waiting—

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Have you?—then pray let it wait,— no! no! Charles—tho' I haven't scrupled to own an affection for you, I have too much respect for the world's opinion,—let us wait with patience,— time may rectify that impetuosity of character, which is now, I own, my dread; think of it, Charles, and beware; for affection is a frail flower, and is reared by the hand of gentleness—it perishes as surely by the shocks of violence as by the more gradual poison of neglect.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Dearest Helen! I will cherish it in my heart—'tis a rough soil I own, but 'tis a warm one; and when the hand of delicacy shall have cultivated this flower that is rooted there, the blossom shall be everlasting love!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Ah you men!—you men! but—I think I may be induced to try you.—Meantime, accept my hand, dear Charles, as a pledge of my heart, and as the assurance that it shall one day be your own indeed
There you needn't eat it—there!—now make your escape, and farewell till we meet again.—

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Zounds! my Father!

div.stage: Enter Sir Rowland and Sir Willoughby, at opposite sides.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Gad a mercy! my papa!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: So, Sir! you are here again I find!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: So! so! Madam! together again, hey? Sir Rowland, your servant.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I need not tell you, Sir Willoughby, that this undutiful boy's conduct does not meet with my sanction.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: No! Sir Willoughby—I am sorry to say my conduct seldom meets with my father's sanction.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Why look ye, Sir Rowland, there are certain things that we do like, and certain things that we do not like—now, Sir, to cut the matter short, I do like my daughter to marry, but I do not like either your son, or your nephew for her husband.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: This is a very sudden change, Sir Willoughby—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Yes, Sir Rowland, I have made two or three sudden changes to day!—I've changed my resolution—I feel changed myself—for I've changed characters with my wife, and with your leave I mean to change my son-in-law.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Of course, Sir, you will give me a proper explanation of the last of these changes.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Sir, if you'll meet me presently at your attorney's, the thing will explain itself—This way, young lady, if you please—Charles, I believe you are a devilish honest fellow, and I want an honest fellow for a son-in-law—but I think it is rather too much to give twelve thousand a year for him— this way Miss Helen.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: This sudden resolution of Sir Willoughby will still more exasperate him—I must seek him instantly, for the crisis of my fate is at hand; my own heart is witness against me—Heaven is my judge, and I have deserved my punishment!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: So! I'm much mistaken, or there'll be a glorious bustle presently at the old lawyer's —He has sent to beg I'll attend, and as my heart is a little at rest in this quarter, I'll e'en see what's going forward in that—whether his intention be to expose or to abet a villain, still I'll be one amongst them; for while I have a heart to feel and a hand to act, I can never be an idle spectator when insulted virtue raises her supplicating voice on one side, and persecution dares to lift his unblushing head on the other.

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: You've done the business, you say!

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Aye, and the parties will all be here presently.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's it! you're sure you haven't blabbed now?

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Blabbed! ha, ha, ha! what do you take me for?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: What do I take you for, Mr. Brass? Why I take you for one that will never be choaked by politeness.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: Why, Lord, Sir, what could a lawyer do without impudence? for tho' they say “honesty's the best policy” a lawyer generally finds his purpose better answered by a Policy of Assurance.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: But hark! somebody's coming already, step where I told you, and make haste.

sp.speaker: Pon.
sp.p: On this occasion I lay by the lawyer and take up the Christian. Benevolence runs fast— but law is lazy and moves slowly.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: I have obeyed your summons! what have you you to say in palliation of the injury you have done me!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Faith and I shall say a small matter about it. What I have done I have performed, and what I have performed I shall justify.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: Indeed! can you justify fraud and villany—To business, Sir—wherefore am I summoned here?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's it!—upon my conscience I'm too modest to tell you.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: Nature and education have made you modest, you were born an Irishman and bred an attorney—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: And take my word for it, when nature forms an Irishman, if she makes some little blunder in the contrivance of his head, it is because she bestows so much pains on the construction of his heart.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: That may be partially true—but to hear you profess sentiments of feeling and justice reminds me of our advertising money-lenders who, while they practice usury and extortion on the world, assure them that “the strictest honor and liberality may be relied on;”—and now, Sir— once more—your business with me—

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Sure, Sir, I sent for you to ask one small bit of a favor.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: From me?!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Aye—from you—and the favor is, that before you honor me with the appellation of scoundrel, villain, pettifogger, and some other such little genteel epithets, you will be pleased to examine my title to such distinctions.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: From you, however, I have no hopes. You have denied your presence at the infamous and sacrilegious mockery of my daughter's marriage.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's a—mistake, Sir—I never did deny it—

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: Ha! you acknowledge it then!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That's another mistake, Sir, for I never did acknowledge it.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
O'Ded.
sp.p: Faith, Sir, tho' you may be a fit representative of the old blind gentlewoman called Justice, she showed little discernment when she pitched upon you and overlooked Mr. Cornelius O'Dedimus, attorney at law. And now, Sir, be pleased to step into that room and wait a moment while I transact a little business with one who is coming yonder.

sp.speaker: Abel Growse.
sp.p: I came hither to obey you, for I have some suspicion of your intentions; and let us hope that one virtuous action, if you have courage to perform it, will serve as a spunge to all the roguery you have committed, either as an attorney or as a man.

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: That blunt little fellow has got a sharp tongue in his head. He's an odd compound; just like a great big roasted potatoe all crusty and crabbed without, but mealy and soft-hearted within—He takes me to be half a rogue and all the rest of me a scoundrel—Och! by St. Patrick! I'll bother his brains presently.

div.stage: Enter Sir Rowland, Lord Austencourt and Charles.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Further discussion, Sir is useless.— If I am to be disappointed in this marriage, a still more strict attention to my own affairs is necessary.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I appeal fearlessly to this man, who has betrayed me, whether your interest was not my sole motive in the appropriation of your property.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: That assertion, Sir, I was prepared to hear, but will not listen to—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Beware, Lord Austencourt, beware how you proceed!—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Do you again threaten me?
are my orders obeyed? is every thing in readiness?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: The officers are in waiting!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Hold, monster—proceed at your peril. —To me you shall answer this atrocious conduct.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: To you?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Aye, Sir, to me, if you have the courage of a man!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I will no longer support these insults —call in the officers!

div.stage: Enter Sir Willoughby, Lady Worrett, and Helen.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Hey! Zounds, did you take me and my Lady Worrett for sheriff's officers, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I have one condition to propose—If that lady accepts my hand I consent to stop the proceedings—that alone can alter my purpose.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Inhuman torturer!

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Were my heart as free as air, I never would consent to a union with such a monster!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: And if you would, curse me if I would —nor my Lady Worrett either.—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Let him fulfil his purpose if he dare! I now see the black corruptness of his heart; and tho' my life were at stake, I would pay the forfeit, rather than immolate innocence in the arms of such depravity.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Call in the officers, I say!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: I shall do that thing!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: 'Tis justice I demand—justice and revenge alike direct me, and their united voice shall be obeyed.

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: They shall! behold me here, thou miscreant to urge it! justice and revenge you call for, and they shall both fall heavily upon you.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Falkner!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: What! Abel Grouse, Mr. Falkner! here's a transmogrification for you!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: How! Falkner, and the unknown Cottager the same person?—

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Aye, Sir! the man who cautioned you to day in vain—who warned you of the precipice beneath your feet, and was unheeded by you—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Amazement! what would you have me do?

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Before this company assist me with the power you possess (and that power is ample) to compel your haughty nephew to repair the injury, which in an humbler character, he has done me—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: He compel me! ridiculous!

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Insensible to injury and insult! can nothing move you?—Reveal your secret!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I'll hear no more,—summon the officers I say—I am resolved!—

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: I too, am at last resolved! at length the arm is raised that, in descending, must crush you.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: I despise your united threats—am I to be the sport of insolence and fraud?—What, am I, Sir, that thus you dare insult me—Who am I?

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: No longer the man you seem to be! hear me! before grief and shame shall burst my heart, hear me proclaim my guilt!—When the late Lord Austencourt dying bequeathed his infant son to my charge, my own child was of the same age! prompted by the dæmons of ambition and blinded to guilt by affection for my own offspring —I CHANGED THE CHILDREN!

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Merciful heaven!

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Hence it follows that you —unnatural monster, are my son!

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Odds life! Hey, then there is something in the world to astonish me, besides the reformation of my Lady Worrett.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Shallow artifice! think you I am weak enough to credit this preposterous fiction, or do you suppose the law will listen to it?—

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: Aye, Sir! the law will listen to it—shall listen to it—I, Sir, can prove the fact beyond even the hesitation of incredulity!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You!

sp.speaker: Falk. I.
sp.p: You have seen me hitherto a poor man, and oppressed me—you see me now rich and powerful, and well prepared to punish your villany; and thus, in every instance, may oppression recoil on the oppressor.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Then I am indeed undone!

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: Shall I call the officers now, my lord? Mr. Austencourt, I should say—I ask pardon for the blunder—and now ladies and gentlemen be pleased to hear me speak—this extraordinary discovery is just exactly what I did not expect. It is true, I had a bit of a discovery of my own to make—for I find that the habits of my profession tho' they haven't led me to commit arts of knavery have too often induced me to wink at them— Therefore, as his quondam Lordship has now certainly lost Miss Helen, I hope he'll have no objection to do justice in another quarter.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Oh, Charles! my much injured nephew! how shall I ever dare to look upon you more?

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Nay, nay, Sir—I am too brimfull of joy at my opening prospects here
to cherish any other feeling than forgiveness and good-humour. Here is my hand, Sir, and with it I pledge myself to oblivion of all the past, except the acts of kindness I have received from you.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: That's a noble, generous young dog— My Lady Worrett, I wonder whether he'll offer to marry Helen now?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Of course, after what has passed, you'll think it decent to refuse for a short time: but you are the best judge, Sir Willoughby, and your will shall in future be mine—

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Shall it—that's kind—then I will refuse him to please you—for when you're so reasonable —how can I do otherwise than oblige you—

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Leave me alone to manage him still.

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: Ah, traitor!

sp.speaker: O'Did.
sp.p: Traitor back again into your teeth, my master! and since you've neither pity for the poor innocent, nor compassion for the little blunt gentleman her father, 'tis time to spake out and to tell you that instead of a sham priest and a sham licence for your deceitful marriage as you bid me, I have sarved the cause of innocence and my own soul, by procuring a real priest and a real licence, and by St. Patrick you are as much one as any two people in England, Ireland, or Scotland!

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Merciful powers! there is still justice for the unfortunate!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: And is this really so?

sp.speaker: O'Ded.
sp.p: You're Man and Wife sure enough— We've decent proof of this too, Sir!

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: You no doubt expect this intelligence will exasperate me. 'Tis the reverse—by Heaven it lifts a load of guilty wretchedness from my heart.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Oh, my lord! my husband!

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: Can this be genuine?—sudden reformation is ever doubtful—

sp.speaker: Lord A.
sp.p: It is real! my errors have been the fruits of an unbridled education—ambition dazzled me, and wealth was my idol. I have acted like a villain, and as my conduct has deserved no forgiveness, so will my degradation be seen without compassion—but this weight of guilt removed, I will seek happiness and virtue in the arms of my much injured Fanny.

sp.speaker: Fanny.
sp.p: Silent joy is the most heartfelt—I cannot speak my happiness! My Father!

sp.speaker: Falkner.
sp.p: This is beyond my hopes; but adversity is a salutary monitor.

sp.speaker: Sir R.
sp.p: Still, Charles, to you I am indebted beyond the power of restitution.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: My dear Father—no—my dear Uncle, I mean. Here is the reward I look for.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: Ah, Charles—(my Lord, I mean, I beg pardon)—to be sure Papa—(aye and mamma-in-law too) will now no longer withhold their consent.

sp.speaker: Sir W.
sp.p: Who me? not for the world—Hey? mercy on us I forgot your Ladyship
do you wish me to decline the honor?

sp.speaker: Lady W.
sp.p: Why no—as matters have turned out.

sp.speaker: Charles.
sp.p: Then Fortune has indeed smiled on me to day!

sp.speaker: Falk.
sp.p: The cloud of sorrow is passed, and may the sun of joy that now illumines my face, diffuse its cheering rays on all around us.

sp.speaker: O'Did.
sp.p: And Sir Willoughby and her ladyship will smile most of us all—for every body knows they're the happiest man and wife among us.

sp.speaker: Helen.
sp.p: And while amongst ourselves we anxious trace The doubtful smile of joy in every face, There is a smile, which doubt and danger ends— The smile of approbation from our friends.
